comparison: Both evaluations support the lack of correlation between prediction scores and tinnitus characteristics (C65-C72) and hearing thresholds (C75, C93, C111). OpenEval notes the exploratory nature and limited sample size, while peer reviewers accept these findings as evidence that hearing loss does not explain group differences.

OpenEval marks speculative mechanistic interpretations (C119-C125) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are hypotheses requiring further testing. Peer reviewers SUPPORT these claims, accepting them as appropriately speculative with one stating 'the authors provide a thoughtful interpretation of their key findings' and 'conclusions are fully supported.' This represents a difference in how speculative interpretations are categorized.

Both agree on successful basic decoding (C53-C58) and no group differences in fundamental auditory processing (C73, C90-C92, C109). OpenEval emphasizes this establishes specificity to predictive processing, while peer reviewers affirm this as foundational to the main findings.

Both support the core finding of group differences in prediction scores (C59-C64, C74). OpenEval notes the p=0.05 threshold concern for one cluster, while peer reviewers emphasize the robustness and describe the evidence as 'compelling' and 'remarkable.'

Both support the replication of prediction score differences in Study 2 (C83-C88, C112-C115, C137-C138). OpenEval highlights the mechanistic insight about control group deactivation, while peer reviewers emphasize the rarity and value of successful replication in tinnitus research.

Both strongly support the Study 2 design with matched hearing thresholds (C28-C34). OpenEval notes this addresses Study 1's major limitation, while peer reviewers call the rigorous matching 'an important strength' ensuring differences cannot be attributed to hearing levels.

Both support the logistic regression analysis showing prediction scores predict tinnitus independent of hearing loss (C101-C107, C108, C110, C132). OpenEval notes the p=0.076 for hearing loss approaches significance, while peer reviewers emphasize this as confirming the matched design's effectiveness.

Both support the equivalence testing showing no group differences in basic auditory processing (C90-C92). OpenEval highlights this as a methodological strength using both null hypothesis and equivalence testing, while peer reviewers accept this as foundational evidence for specificity to predictive processing.

Both support the comparison of effect sizes across studies using Bayes factors (C95-C98). OpenEval notes the frequency range interpretation remains speculative, while peer reviewers accept the authors' explanations for reduced effect sizes as plausible.

Both support the finding that frequency spacing affected decoding accuracy (C81-C82). OpenEval notes the mechanistic explanation is reasonable but interpretive, while peer reviewers accept this as part of plausible explanations for methodological differences between studies.

Both support the trial number analysis (C99-C100). OpenEval notes the post-hoc subsampling limitation, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the authors' plausible explanations for effect size differences.

Both support the methodological recommendations for future studies (C129-C130). OpenEval emphasizes these are evidence-based from systematic parameter analysis, while peer reviewers accept these as part of thoughtful interpretation and future directions.

Both support the inference about frequency spacing effects on prediction scores (C127-C128). OpenEval bases this on the decoding accuracy findings, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the methodological interpretation.

Both strongly support the significance of replication (C131, C133-C134, C139). OpenEval emphasizes the demonstration of generalizability, while peer reviewers highlight replication as 'remarkable' and 'rare in the tinnitus field,' describing the evidence as 'compelling.'

Both support the mechanistic interpretations (C116-C118) with appropriate caveats. OpenEval notes the speculative nature of late training interval interpretations, while peer reviewers accept these as thoughtful interpretations that are appropriately acknowledged as speculative.

Both support the summary conclusions and future directions (C135-C136, C140). OpenEval emphasizes the data-driven support for below-chance decoding and appropriate scientific self-correction, while peer reviewers note 'conclusions are fully supported' and 'limitations are clearly addressed.'

Both support successful decoding in Study 2 (C77-C80). OpenEval emphasizes source localization validity, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the foundational evidence for the main predictive processing findings.

Both support the main findings summary (C108-C112). OpenEval notes the replication and exclusion of confounds are well-supported, while peer reviewers emphasize the compelling nature of the replicated evidence.

Both support the Study 1 summary findings (C73-C75). OpenEval cautions about the hearing threshold conclusion given lack of audiometric data for controls, while peer reviewers accept these as part of the overall supported findings.

Both support the null findings for correlations in Study 2 (C93-C94). OpenEval notes limited power from reduced sample size, while peer reviewers accept these as evidence that hearing loss does not explain group differences.

OpenEval supports the background epidemiological and clinical characterizations of tinnitus (C1-C5) as well-cited and widely accepted. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these introductory claims.

OpenEval supports the background on hearing loss-tinnitus association and mechanistic theory limitations (C6-C14) as appropriately cited. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these introductory claims.

OpenEval supports the theoretical framework description and acknowledgment of limited empirical support (C15-C21). No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these theoretical background claims.

OpenEval supports the Study 1 participant descriptions (C22-C27), noting the explicit acknowledgment of lacking audiometric data for controls. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific methodological details.
OpenEval supports the detailed experimental stimuli and design descriptions (C35-C43). No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific methodological details.
OpenEval supports the MEG acquisition and preprocessing procedures (C44-C50) as standard and well-cited. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these technical methodological details.
OpenEval supports the MVPA methods description (C51-C52) as standard and appropriately cited. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these technical methodological details.

Peer reviewers support the overall replication and robustness of findings (C76, C108, C131, C133-C134, C139), emphasizing this as rare and valuable in tinnitus research. While OpenEval addresses these claims across multiple results (R21, R26), peer reviewers group them as a unified strength of the study.
